analysis.one_liner: Blocks generic competition with a single brand-name drug for five to seven years.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee and its antitrust subcommittee until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995, after drawing only two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the rules for generic drug approval so that a drug meeting five very specific conditions — an application filed before September 1982, under FDA review for at least 78 months, and approved on October 29, 1992 — would be shielded from generic competition for 5 years from approval, plus up to 24 more months to make up for the unusually long FDA review. Those conditions are so precise that they describe one particular brand-name drug. The result would be several more years during which no cheaper generic version could be submitted or approved for that drug.
analysis.who_benefits: The maker of the one brand-name drug that matches the bill's criteria would gain years of guaranteed protection from generic competitors, allowing it to keep charging brand-name prices long after the normal framework for market exclusivity had run its course. The bill would essentially grant that company a legislative extension of its monopoly.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars the FDA from accepting or approving any generic application (abbreviated new drug application) that refers to the qualifying drug for 5 years from its October 1992 approval, plus up to 24 additional months tied to the length of the FDA review, keeping generics off the market during that window [S3].

It applies only to a drug whose application was filed before September 1, 1982, spent at least 78 months under regulatory review, and was approved on October 29, 1992 — conditions narrow enough to fit a single product [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients who need the drug, along with their insurers, employers, and government programs like Medicare and Medicaid, would pay brand-name prices for years longer instead of switching to cheaper generic equivalents once those become legally available.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients, insurers, and government drug buyers

drawbacks.text: Extending exclusivity by statute would delay cheaper generic versions of the drug, raising costs for patients and for public and private health payers during the extra years of protection [S3].

The bill's five criteria are so specific that they fit a single drug, meaning Congress would be writing a custom commercial benefit for one company into law rather than setting a general rule — a precedent other manufacturers could seek through the same route [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the existing Hatch-Waxman framework already provides periods of market exclusivity and patent-term restoration for long FDA reviews, so the bill would add a layer of protection on top of what the general law provides.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain is concentrated on one drug company in the form of extended monopoly pricing; the cost is spread across everyone who buys or pays for that drug through higher prices for years longer. The bill offers no corresponding benefit to consumers, and its drug-specific drafting makes it a bespoke favor rather than a policy.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee referred the bill to its antitrust subcommittee in February 1994, where it sat without a markup or vote until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. Paul Simon introduced the bill on November 20, 1993, joined by Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-UT) and Sen. Carol Moseley-Braun (D-IL) [S1] [S3] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on November 20, 1993 [S5].
On February 3, 1994, the Judiciary Committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Antitrust, Monopolies and Business — the last action recorded [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, never reaching a committee vote or a floor vote [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, patients, insurers, and government programs were spared years of paying brand-name prices for a drug that would otherwise have faced generic competition; generic manufacturers also retained access to that market. The sponsoring company did not get its legislated exclusivity extension.

for.name: Sen. Paul Simon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Market Exclusivity Act of 1993 in the Senate [S1] [S5].

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to its Subcommittee on Antitrust, Monopolies and Business on February 3, 1994, and never scheduled a markup or vote [S5].

against.name: Subcommittee on Antitrust, Monopolies and Business
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from February 1994 until the Congress ended without any action [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and one cosponsor were Democrats and the other cosponsor was a Republican, so sponsorship was bipartisan, but there were no votes on the bill from which to judge party alignment.

industries.note: The bill would grant years of extra protection from generic competition to one company's drug, letting it keep brand-name pricing long after normal exclusivity rules had run. Every year of that delay is higher prices for patients and payers.

The bill would bar the FDA from accepting or approving generic applications for the covered drug for the exclusivity period, keeping generic firms out of that market. Its failure preserved their access.

industries.industry: Health insurers and public drug payers (Medicare, Medicaid)
industries.note: Payers would bear the higher brand-name prices during the extended exclusivity window, either directly through program spending or indirectly through premiums. The bill's failure avoided that cost.
